chunks.authors: Thomas Uriot, Dario Izzo, Luis F. Simoes, Rasit Abay, Nils Einecke, Sven Rebhan, Jose Martinez-Heras, Francesca Letizia, Jan Siminski, Klaus Merz
chunks.text: The Spacecraft Collision Avoidance Challenge enabled, for the first time, the study of the use of ML methods in the domain of spacecraft collision avoidance owing to the public release of a unique dataset collected by the ESA Space Debris Office over more than four years of operations. Several challenges, mostly derived from the unavoidable unbalanced nature of the dataset, had to be accounted for to release the dataset in the form of a competition and the use of automated, off-the-shelf ML pipelines were limited. Nevertheless, the competition results and further experiments presented here clearly demonstrated two things. On one hand, naive forecasting models have surprisingly good performances and thus are established as an unavoidable benchmark for any future work in this subject; on the other hand, ML models can improve upon such a benchmark, hinting at the possibility of using ML to improve the decision-making process in collision avoidance systems.

chunks.authors: Giacomo Acciarini, Francesco Pinto, Francesca Letizia, Jose A. Martinez-Heras, Klaus Merz, Christopher Bridges, Atilim Gunes Baydin
chunks.text: In previous work [37] we discuss that approaching the spacecraft collision avoidance problem as discriminative binary-classification formulation in ML (i.e., high- vs low-risk events) has various shortcomings (e.g., training data class imbalance, scarce interpretability of the output). For this reason, we focus our attention on the generative modeling of the problem, in other words we would like to deliver ML methods that describe the temporal evolution of a sequence of CDMs given all previously observed CDMs.

chunks.authors: Giacomo Acciarini, Francesco Pinto, Francesca Letizia, Jose A. Martinez-Heras, Klaus Merz, Christopher Bridges, Atilim Gunes Baydin
chunks.text: We believe that ML approaches will be essential in improving collision avoidance analyses and decision making processes in the near future and enable scalable automated systems that would greatly enhance the collision avoidance process, with positive consequences for the safeguarding of the space environment. Following up on the ESA studies, we develop Kessler (Figure 1) a ML library for spacecraft collision avoidance, that we named in honor of the NASA scientist Donald J. Kessler known for proposing the Kessler syndrome. To deliver maximum benefit to the space and ML communities, we release Kessler as an open-source project that we expect to keep improving following this initial release and to which we welcome contributions from the wider community.

chunks.authors: Joao Simoes Catulo, Claudia Soares, Marta Guimaraes
chunks.text: In 2019, the European Space Agency (ESA) launched the Collision Avoidance Challenge (CAC) [5] to study the feasibility of applying machine learning (ML) methods in collision risk estimation and released a dataset that contained sequences of CDMs received in support of real close encounters. The competition aimed to develop ML models capable of predicting the criticality of conjunction events by analysing the time series of CDMs received up to 2 days before the predicted TCA, which is considered the cut-off time. The collision probability within the CDMs is computed through the Alfriend-Akella algorithm [6] and the final risk of each event is considered to be the risk contained in the last released CDM, which is the best knowledge about the outcome of the close approach. Figure 2 illustrates the concept of ML in collision avoidance.

chunks.authors: Thomas Uriot, Dario Izzo, Luis F. Simoes, Rasit Abay, Nils Einecke, Sven Rebhan, Jose Martinez-Heras, Francesca Letizia, Jan Siminski, Klaus Merz
chunks.text: Further ML experiments were conducted on the dataset, both to analyze the competition and to further investigate the use of predictive models for collision avoidance. The aim of these experiments was to understand the difficulties experienced by competitors in this challenge and to gain deeper insights into the ability of ML models to learn generalizable knowledge from these data.

chunks.authors: Thomas Uriot, Dario Izzo, Luis F. Simoes, Rasit Abay, Nils Einecke, Sven Rebhan, Jose Martinez-Heras, Francesca Letizia, Jan Siminski, Klaus Merz
chunks.text: The database of conjunction events constitutes an important historical record of risky conjunction events that occurred in LEO and creates the opportunity to test the use of ML approaches in the collision avoidance process. The decision on whether to perform an avoidance maneuver is based on the best knowledge one has of the associated collision risk at the time when the maneuver cannot be further delayed, i.e., the risk reported in the latest CDM available. Such a decision would clearly benefit from a forecast of the collision risk, enabling past evolution and projected trends to be considered. During the design of the Spacecraft Collision Avoidance Challenge, it was natural to begin from a forecasting standpoint, seeking an answer to the question: can an ML model forecast the collision risk evolution from available CDMs?

chunks.authors: Joao Simoes Catulo, Claudia Soares, Marta Guimaraes
chunks.text: After the competition, relevant work regarding the use of ML in collision avoidance has been conducted. Metz [9] implemented various models to predict the final chaser position uncertainties for each event and used those predictions to compute the risk using Akella's and Alfriend's algorithm [6]. Acciarini et al. [10] built a physics-based generative model using probabilistic programming to simulate the generation of CDMs, based on real data. Pinto et al. [11] used Bayesian deep learning with recurrent neural network architectures to also study the possibility of generating CDMs. Abay et al. [12] benchmarked the results for the state-of-the-art ML models that showed good results against the naive approach since the beginning of the competition.

chunks.authors: Giacomo Acciarini, Francesco Pinto, Francesca Letizia, Jose A. Martinez-Heras, Klaus Merz, Christopher Bridges, Atilim Gunes Baydin
chunks.text: In this work we present Kessler: an open-source Python package for machine learning (ML) applied to collision avoidance. Kessler provides functionalities to import and export conjunction data messages (CDMs) in their standard format and predict the evolution of conjunction events based on explainable ML models.

chunks.authors: Thomas Uriot, Dario Izzo, Luis F. Simoes, Rasit Abay, Nils Einecke, Sven Rebhan, Jose Martinez-Heras, Francesca Letizia, Jan Siminski, Klaus Merz
chunks.text: To advance the research on the automation of preventive collision avoidance maneuvers, the European Space Agency (ESA) released a unique real-world dataset containing a time series of events representing the evolution of collision risks related to several actively monitored satellites. The dataset was made available to the public as part of a machine learning (ML) challenge called the Collision Avoidance Challenge, which was hosted on the Kelvins online platform. The challenge occurred over two months, with 96 teams participating, resulting in 862 submissions. It attracted a wide range of people, from students to ML practitioners and aerospace engineers, as well as academic institutions and companies.

chunks.authors: Alinda K. Mashiku, Lauri K. Newman, Dolan E. Highsmith
chunks.text: While AI/ML approaches investigated to date have not yet demonstrated sufficient reliability for operational collision avoidance decision making, several promising directions for future research remain. Although beyond CARA's direct purview, AI/ML techniques could potentially be applied to improve conjunction screening processes through development of adaptive screening volumes that optimize computational resources while maintaining safety margins. As noted in [16], investigating Recurring Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTM models to ingest time-series based information could eventually provide more reliable predictions at TCA, especially if approaches can be developed that incorporate uncertainty quantification in the predictions. Future studies should carefully consider that predictions of future measurement updates are nearly impossible to model deterministically since they are not entirely physics-based, and that routine maneuvers as part of normal operations are difficult or impossible to model or incorporate within a model. These critical limitations must be addressed by any AI/ML approach for it to be operationally viable.

generation.answer:
Based on the provided evidence, several main failure modes and limitations of ML for collision avoidance can be identified:

## Dataset Imbalance and Competition Challenges

The primary failure mode stems from the **unavoidable unbalanced nature of the dataset** used for training ML models (uriot2022, sec7_p1). This imbalance creates significant challenges, as the dataset contains far more low-risk events than high-risk collision events, making it difficult for ML models to learn effective discrimination patterns.

Related to this, **discriminative binary-classification formulations** (high-risk vs. low-risk events) have been shown to have various shortcomings, including training data class imbalance and scarce interpretability of outputs (acciarini2021, sec3.1_p1).

## Limitations of Automated Approaches

The dataset imbalance and other challenges meant that **the use of automated, off-the-shelf ML pipelines were limited** in their effectiveness (uriot2022, sec7_p1). This suggests that simple application of standard ML techniques is insufficient for this domain.

## Physics-Based Modeling Limitations

A critical failure mode identified is that **predictions of future measurement updates are nearly impossible to model deterministically since they are not entirely physics-based** (mashiku2025, sec6_p1). This fundamental limitation means that ML models struggle to accurately forecast how measurements will evolve over time.

Additionally, **routine maneuvers as part of normal operations are difficult or impossible to model or incorporate within a model** (mashiku2025, sec6_p1). This represents a significant gap in ML capabilities, as operational spacecraft frequently perform planned maneuvers that affect collision risk.

## Reliability for Operational Use

Perhaps most critically, **AI/ML approaches investigated to date have not yet demonstrated sufficient reliability for operational collision avoidance decision making** (mashiku2025, sec6_p1). This indicates that despite research progress, ML methods have not reached the threshold of trustworthiness required for real-world deployment in safety-critical collision avoidance systems.

## Missing Information

The evidence does not provide detailed information on:
- Specific false positive/false negative rates
- Model overfitting or generalization failures
- Temporal drift in model performance
- Specific architectural limitations of different ML approaches
- Quantitative metrics on prediction accuracy degradation

Sources discussing uncertainty quantification methods, comparative performance metrics across different ML architectures, and specific operational failure case studies would help provide a more complete picture of ML failure modes in this domain.

## REFERENCES
uriot2022 — Spacecraft Collision Avoidance Challenge (2022)
acciarini2021 — Bayesian ML for spacecraft conjunctions (2021)
mashiku2025 — Future Directions and Conclusions (2025)

chunks.text: Since the goal of ML models in the collision probability assessment is to analyse the sequence of the values of the collision risk (the base-10 logarithm of the collision probability) contained in the CDMs received until the cut-off time and correctly identify whether an event is of high or low risk of collision, the data can be divided into two categorical classes, based on the risk that is present in the last CDM released in each event: if the risk is lower than −6, the event is considered of low risk, otherwise it is considered a high-risk event. This was the threshold defined during the CAC [7] and, since the same dataset is used and in order to better compare the obtained results, the same threshold is chosen in this work. Thus, in the dataset there are 12789 low-risk events (97.23%) and only 365 high-risk conjunctions (2.77%), highlighting the rare occurrence of high-risk events. The data imbalance problem poses to be the main challenge in collision risk estimation using ML methods. It is also important to note that the values of the risk contained in the CDMs are truncated at a lower bound of −30, in other words, the probability is truncated at 10⁻³⁰. A closer look into the data showed that 63.5% of the total number of conjunction events has a final risk of −30, i.e., represent false alerts.

chunks.section_title: Identification of Parameters Associated with High-Risk Events
chunks.authors: Alinda K. Mashiku, Lauri K. Newman, Dolan E. Highsmith
chunks.text: The investigation yielded several insights regarding which parameters showed the strongest association with high-risk conjunction events. Across both supervised and unsupervised approaches, the miss distance parameter (obviously, since this is about collision avoidance - avoiding close proximity) consistently emerged as the most significant parameter correlated with collision risk, followed by probability of collision (Pc), approach angle, and relative velocity. The hierarchical clustering and competitive network analyses revealed strong correlations between miss distance and Mahalanobis distance metrics, suggesting that these statistical measures capture similar aspects of conjunction geometry relevant to risk assessment.

chunks.authors: Alinda K. Mashiku, Lauri K. Newman, Dolan E. Highsmith
chunks.text: Recommendations for continued improvements on conjunction assessment processes may focus on addressing fundamental data limitations and physics-based constraints on data quality. A key recommendation involves improving covariance realism, as unrealistic covariance matrices fundamentally undermine the reliability of any risk assessment approach in addition to any machine learning model. Additionally, the development of weighted loss functions that address the class imbalance problem by giving higher importance to the rare high-risk events could improve model training outcomes if implemented carefully. Perhaps most importantly, future work should focus on explainable AI techniques that provide transparency into how models arrive at risk assessments, making them more trustworthy for operational decision making where accountability is essential.

chunks.text: To establish an ML performance baseline, we now turn directly to the F2 score rather than its inverse (see the discussion in Section 4.3). F2, which ranges in [0, 1], is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, where recall (ability to identify all high-risk events) is valued two times higher than precision (ability to ensure all events predicted as being of high-risk indeed are). A Monte Carlo cross-validation with a test size of 0.2 and 505 stratified random data splits evaluated the LRP baseline (the direct use of an event's latest CDM's risk value as prediction) to a mean F2 score of 0.59967 over the test set (standard deviation: 0.04391). Over the same data splits, a LightGBM regressor, acting over the same CDM raw values (see data and model configurations in Section 6.1), evaluated to a mean F2 score of 0.60732 over the test set (standard deviation: 0.04895; statistics over 50500 trained models). Therefore, a gain of 1.2743% over the LRP baseline. The difference in performance between both approaches is statistically significant: a paired Student's t-test rejects the null hypothesis of equal averages (t-statistic: âˆ’10.23, two-sided p-value: 1.83 x 10^âˆ’22; per data split, the LRP F2 score was paired with the mean LightGBM model F2 score to ensure independence across pairs).

Based on the evidence provided, the class imbalance ratio between high-risk and low-risk conjunction events varies depending on the specific dataset version and risk threshold used:

## Main Dataset (Pre-cleaning)

In the original dataset analyzed by Catulo et al., there were **12,789 low-risk events (97.23%) and 365 high-risk events (2.77%)** when using a risk threshold of -6 (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3). This represents an imbalance ratio of approximately **35:1** in favor of low-risk events.

## After Data Cleaning

Following data cleaning procedures, the imbalance became even more severe. The cleaned dataset contained **7,187 low-risk events (99.3%) and only 50 high-risk events (0.7%)** (catulo2023, sec3.2_p2). This represents an imbalance ratio of approximately **144:1** in favor of low-risk events.

## Alternative Dataset Version

A different version of the dataset, analyzed by Uriot et al., contained **15,321 total events**, with the number of high-risk events varying by risk threshold:
- 30 high-risk events at r ≥ 10⁻⁴
- 131 high-risk events at r ≥ 10⁻⁵  
- 515 high-risk events at r ≥ 10⁻⁶ (uriot2022, sec3_p4)

Using the 10⁻⁶ threshold (equivalent to risk of -6), this represents approximately **515 high-risk events out of 15,321 total events (3.36%)**, giving an imbalance ratio of approximately **29:1**.

## Additional Context

The evidence emphasizes that this severe class imbalance "poses to be the major challenge" of collision risk estimation using ML methods (catulo2023, sec3.2_p2). Additionally, 63.5% of conjunction events had a final risk of -30 (the lower truncation bound), representing false alerts (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3).

---

In the original database, there were **15,321 total events**, with only **30 high-risk events (risk ≥ 10⁻⁴)** representing the most stringent threshold (uriot2022, sec3_p4). This represents approximately 0.2% high-risk events at this threshold.

# Catastrophic Forgetting in Orbit Decay Prediction

## The Problem

Catastrophic forgetting represents a significant challenge for machine learning models in orbit decay prediction. According to He et al., "the dynamic factors influencing the decay, such as the space environment and spacecraft physical parameters, pose a challenge of catastrophic forgetting for conventional MLT" (he2024, sec1_p6). This phenomenon limits the generalization capabilities of current model-agnostic machine learning techniques (he2024, sec1_p6).

The evidence indicates that catastrophic forgetting is specifically problematic in the context of Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) spacecraft, where the generalization performance of machine learning techniques "is blocked by the universal challenge known as catastrophic forgetting, resulting in limited improvement on PODP [precise orbit decay prediction]" (he2024, sec0_p1).

## He 2024's Solution: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)

To address catastrophic forgetting, He et al. propose using Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) as part of their Expandable Orbit Decay Propagator (EODP) method. The study explains that "EODP employs a deep NN (DNN) as the fundamental learner to comprehend the decaying rule and incorporates the theory of EWC" (he2024, sec1_p7).

The rationale for selecting EWC is explained in their discussion of various strategies to enhance neural network generalization performance. They note that "EWC combines historical and recent training data to update the NN parameters by applying a penalty function, commonly used to process large datasets by decomposing them into several subsets in the field of earth observation" (he2024, sec1_p6). Importantly, they identify that "EWC is particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data" (he2024, sec1_p6), which aligns well with the orbit decay prediction problem.

## Context and Alternative Approaches

The evidence also mentions alternative strategies that were considered but not selected for this application. Meta-learning "seeks to achieve 'learning to learn,' allowing NN to be flexible and adaptable in various scenarios" and "excels in few-shot learning" (he2024, sec1_p6). Experience replay "involves the creation of a small memory buffer to retain samples from previous tasks" and "efficiently constructs and utilizes memory buffers with a limited sample size" (he2024, sec1_p6). However, given the nature of orbit decay prediction as a regression problem with abundant data, EWC was the most appropriate choice.

## Outcomes

The implementation of EODP with EWC achieved significant improvements, with "the model achiev[ing] at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP)" (he2024, sec0_p1).

In recent years, several methods with machine learning techniques (MLTs) have emerged to enhance the capabilities of TOPM. Cimmino, Opromolla, and Fasano [11] used MLT to determine the ballistic coefficients of LEO spacecraft based on orbital data. Lei and Zhang [12] employed another form of proximal policy optimization, PPO2, to adjust atmosphere model parameters to improve TOPM. Compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP), the proposed approach significantly reduced residual errors. Li et al. The effectiveness of the traditional orbital prediction method for PODP is limited by inaccurate estimation of the spacecraft's physical parameters and space environments. Generalization performance of machine learning techniques (MLTs) is blocked by the universal challenge known as catastrophic forgetting, resulting in limited improvement on PODP. In this study, a method of expandable orbit decay propagator (EODP) for spacecraft PODP in VLEO, based on model-agnostic MLTs, is proposed. The plasticity of the proposed model is discussed, which originates from the uncertainty of neural network (NN) parameters. The proposed method overcomes the negative effects of uncertain physical parameters and complex space environments. The model achieves at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP) and presents a novel approach for the future implementation of machine learning–based methods in the field of orbit prediction.

# Impact of Extreme Rarity of Collision Events on ML Model Training and Validation

## Severe Class Imbalance Problem

The extreme rarity of collision events creates a fundamental challenge for ML model training. The dataset used across multiple studies shows that only 2.77% of events (365 out of 13,154) are classified as high-risk conjunctions, while 97.23% (12,789 events) are low-risk (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3). This severe class imbalance is identified as "the main challenge in collision risk estimation using ML methods" (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3).

The imbalance is even more extreme when examining the data distribution: 63.5% of all conjunction events have a final risk value truncated at -30 (the lower bound), representing false alerts (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3). This means that the vast majority of training data represents extremely low-risk scenarios, making it difficult for supervised learning models to learn patterns associated with genuinely dangerous encounters.

## Training Challenges

The rarity of actual collision events creates multiple training difficulties:

1. **Difficulty in Pattern Recognition**: The scarcity of collision events makes it "difficult to train supervised learning models that could accurately distinguish between safe and unsafe encounters" (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p1).

2. **Inconsistent Behavioral Patterns**: The problem is compounded by the fact that "sample cases generated from the same baseline often exhibited completely different behavioral patterns, undermining the assumption that historical patterns could reliably predict future conjunction evolution" (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p1). This inconsistency, combined with rarity, means there are few examples and those examples don't follow predictable patterns.

3. **Stochastic Nature**: The "stochastic and non-linear nature of the conjunction evolution created inconsistent parameter behavior patterns that were difficult for machine learning models to capture reliably" (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p1).

## Mitigation Strategies

Researchers have attempted to address the class imbalance through data preparation strategies. One approach involves removing the most extreme low-risk cases from training: when a naive forecast predicts a final risk of -30, 99.34% of predictions are correct with no misclassification of high-risk events (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1). By excluding these -30 predictions from training and directly predicting them as -30 during testing, researchers can "deal with the data imbalance problem" while also reducing memory requirements and computational time (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1).

Additionally, data vectorization techniques are employed to handle the variable number of CDMs (Conjunction Data Messages) per event, with sequences being standardized by repeating CDMs to ensure uniform input dimensions for training (catulo2023, sec3.3_p4).

## Validation Challenges

The rarity of collision events also affects validation approaches. The evidence notes that "comprehensive collision datasets remain limited," requiring researchers to rely on "theoretical assessment of close conjunction events characterized by non-zero miss distances" as "a viable foundation for evaluating the operational validity of AI/ML implementation" (mashiku2025, sec2_p5). This suggests that validation must often occur on near-miss events rather than actual collisions, which may not fully represent the characteristics of true collision scenarios.

The European Space Agency's Collision Avoidance Challenge was specifically designed to "study the feasibility of applying machine learning (ML) methods in collision risk estimation" using a curated dataset spanning 2015-2019 (uriot2022, sec0_p1). The competition aimed to develop models capable of predicting conjunction event criticality, with the understanding that the final risk in the last released CDM represents "the best knowledge about the outcome of the close approach" (catulo2023, sec1_p5). However, the fundamental challenge remains that actual collision ground truth is scarce.

## Critical Gap in Evidence

While the evidence clearly documents the class imbalance problem and its impact on training, there is insufficient detail about how the rarity specifically affects validation metrics, false positive/false negative tradeoffs, or how researchers determine if their models would actually perform well on real collision events given the limited availability of such cases in validation sets.

To be tractable, these algorithms hold simplifying assumptions that hinder accuracy [2]. Each method is limited by OD in that an orbital state with high uncertainty will necessarily evolve to have an inaccurate Orbit Prediction. When used in a Collision Avoidance scheme, this process propagates the state of the RSO until the time of closest approach (TCA) to any actively monitored satellite. # ML Architectures Applied to CDM Time-Series Prediction and Their Failure Modes

## Architectures Applied

Several ML architectures have been applied to the CDM time-series prediction problem:

### 1. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks

LSTM networks, a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that retains memory about inputs and utilizes that memory to predict outcomes on time-dependent series, have been implemented to handle the time-varying nature of CDM data as conjunction assessments evolve toward TCA (mashiku2025, sec3.4_p1). Bayesian recurrent neural networks (specifically stacked LSTM architectures) have been designed to predict future CDMs in conjunction events, with the network returning distributions rather than point predictions due to their Bayesian nature (acciarini2021, sec4.2_p2). Manhattan LSTMs showed good performance during the Collision Avoidance Challenge (catulo2023, sec1_p6).

### 2. Shallow Neural Networks

Shallow binary classification networks have been applied, with models incorporating multiple information parameters beyond just collision probability (Pc) (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 3. Deep Neural Networks

Deep Neural Networks have been applied to static CDM analysis (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 4. Gradient Boosting Trees

Gradient boosting trees (specifically LightGBM) showed good performance during the Collision Avoidance Challenge (catulo2023, sec1_p6). These were applied without transformations to CDM raw values such as scaling or embedding, and without steps to impute missing values (uriot2022, sec6.1_p1).

### 5. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs)

HMMs have been applied to analyze CDM time series arranged in descending order regarding time to TCA (catulo2023, sec3.3_p3).

## Comparison of Failure Modes

### LSTM Failure Modes

**Insufficient Training Data and Poor Generalization**: The LSTM models designed for time-series prediction suffered from insufficient "ground truth data" for training and poor generalization to diverse conjunction scenarios (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

**Long-term Prediction Degradation**: For long-term forecasting (around 100 years), both overlapping and non-overlapping LSTM strategies failed dramatically, reaching loss values six orders of magnitude larger than short-term benchmarks. The overlapping approach showed huge increases in the loss function especially in the first year. The degradation is attributed to the number of iterations needed to span long periods of time (mocat_ml2024, sec5.2_p4).

### Shallow Neural Network Failure Modes

**Marginal Improvements**: Shallow binary classification networks showed only marginal improvements in risk classification when incorporating multiple information parameters beyond just Pc. The improvement appeared extremely marginal compared to using normal Pc thresholds, raising questions about the practical value of the additional computational complexity (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

**Linear Complexity Limitations**: Shallow neural networks are susceptible to errors from highly nonlinear coupling due to operating at a linear level of complexity (mashiku2025, sec3.4_p1).

### Deep Neural Network Failure Modes

**Lack of Memory**: Standard neural networks (either shallow or deep) do not remember or account for previous time-series inputs but only focus on the immediate past data during the training phase (mashiku2025, sec3.4_p1).

### General Observation Across Architectures

**Limited Use of Temporal Information**: Surprisingly, 65% of teams in the Collision Avoidance Challenge framed the learning problem as a static one, summarizing the information contained in the time series as an aggregation of attributes (e.g., using summary statistics, or simply the latest available CDM) rather than utilizing temporal evolution (uriot2022, sec5.1_p4). This suggests that many ML approaches failed to effectively leverage the temporal structure of CDM data, possibly because the naive forecast (using the last CDM as the prediction) proved to be a strong predictor, with only 12 teams out of 97 managing to beat the benchmark solution (catulo2023, sec1_p6).

## Missing Information

The evidence provided does not include:
- Quantitative comparison metrics (e.g., specific accuracy, F1 scores, or loss values) across different architectures
- Detailed analysis of failure modes for gradient boosting trees and HMMs
- Information about ensemble methods or hybrid architectures
- Specific error patterns or failure scenarios for each architecture type

Sources that might provide additional comparative analysis of specific failure scenarios and quantitative performance metrics would help complete this assessment.

# Catastrophic Forgetting in Orbit Decay Prediction

## The Challenge of Catastrophic Forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting poses a significant challenge for machine learning techniques (MLTs) applied to orbit decay prediction. According to He et al., the dynamic factors influencing orbital decay, such as the space environment and spacecraft physical parameters, create a challenge of catastrophic forgetting for conventional MLT (he2024, sec1_p6). More specifically, the generalization performance of machine learning techniques is "blocked by the universal challenge known as catastrophic forgetting, resulting in limited improvement on PODP [precise orbit decay prediction]" (he2024, sec0_p1).

The issue appears to stem from the varying conditions that MLTs must handle in orbit prediction scenarios. Current model-agnostic MLTs face limitations in their generalization capabilities due to this phenomenon (he2024, sec1_p6).

## He 2024's Solution: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)

To address catastrophic forgetting, He et al. employ **Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)** as part of their Expandable Orbit Decay Propagator (EODP) method. The EODP "employs a deep NN (DNN) as the fundamental learner to comprehend the decaying rule and incorporates the theory of EWC" (he2024, sec1_p7).

EWC is described as a regularization-based approach that "combines historical and recent training data to update the NN parameters by applying a penalty function" (he2024, sec1_p6). The authors note that EWC is "particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data" (he2024, sec1_p6), which aligns with the characteristics of orbit decay prediction problems where historical orbital data can be extensive.

## Rationale for Choosing EWC

He et al. considered multiple strategies to enhance generalization performance of neural networks, including:
- Optimization-based methods (like meta-learning)
- Replay-based techniques (such as experience replay)
- Regularization-based approaches (like EWC)

They chose EWC over alternatives because "meta-learning methods excel in few-shot learning, and experience replay efficiently constructs and utilizes memory buffers with a limited sample size. EWC is particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data" (he2024, sec1_p6).

## Results

The proposed EODP method "achieves at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP)" (he2024, sec0_p1), and compared to previous methods, "EODP greatly improves prediction accuracy and generalization performance" (he2024, sec1_p7).

chunks.text: Satellite conjunctions are approaches between two satellites closer than a specified set of distances, which is often chosen to be much larger than the set that would pose an actual collision threat. A key next step, therefore, is to evaluate each conjunction to determine if it poses, or is likely to pose, a substantial risk of collision. This evaluation activity, called conjunction risk assessment, comprises both the key calculations that feed the concept of risk (that is, both collision likelihood and collision consequence) and the evaluations of the input data that subtend these calculations to ensure that they constitute a basis for decision making. Only conjunctions that are determined to be high risk merit the consideration of mitigation actions.

Based on the provided evidence, I can identify the following data quality issues and preparation steps taken with the ESA conjunction data messages used for the Collision Avoidance Challenge:

## Data Quality Issues and Filtering

The ESA dataset required significant data cleaning and filtering before use. According to the evidence, several categories of problematic entries were identified and removed:

1. **Low theoretical risk events**: Events where the theoretical maximum collision probability was less than 10^-15 were excluded (uriot2022, sec3_p1).

2. **Intra-constellation conjunctions**: Events related to conjunctions between satellites within the same constellation (e.g., for the Cluster II mission) were removed (uriot2022, sec3_p1).

3. **Anomalous entries**: The dataset contained anomalous entries, specifically scenarios with null relative velocity between the target and chaser, which were removed (uriot2022, sec3_p1).

4. **Maneuver-related data**: Events that covered periods during which the spacecraft performed a maneuver posed prediction problems. The last estimation of collision risk could not be predicted from the evolution of the CDM data because the propulsive maneuver was not described in the data. These scenarios were addressed by removing all CDM data before the maneuver epoch (uriot2022, sec3_p1).

## Dataset Characteristics

The final dataset used for the challenge consisted of CDMs collected between 2015 and 2019, containing 162,634 samples/CDMs with 103 parameters each, representing 13,154 unique conjunction events (catulo2023, sec3.1_p1).

chunks.text: Recognition of space objects including spacecraft and debris is one of the main components in the space situational awareness (SSA) system. The conditions include various backgrounds affected by noise, several orbital scenarios, high contrast, low signal-to-noise ratio, and various object sizes. To extract features from RGB images that have spacecraft and debris, various convolutional neural network (CNN) based models such as ResNet, EfficientNet, and DenseNet were explored. Furthermore, RGB based vision transformer was demonstrated. Additionally, End-to-End CNN was used for classification of depth images. The final decision of the proposed solution combines the two decisions from RGB based and Depth-based models. The dataset includes various images with eleven categories, and it is divided into 150 k of RGB images and 150 k of depth images. # Impact of Extreme Rarity of Collision Events on ML Model Training and Validation

The extreme rarity of actual collision events creates severe challenges for both training and validation of machine learning models in collision avoidance systems, manifesting in multiple interconnected failure modes.

## Class Imbalance Problem

The dataset exhibits dramatic class imbalance. In the ESA collision avoidance challenge dataset, there are only 365 high-risk conjunctions (2.77%) compared to 12,789 low-risk events (97.23%), with 63.5% of all conjunction events having a final risk of -30 (representing false alerts) (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3). This severe imbalance is explicitly identified as "the main challenge in collision risk estimation using ML methods" (catulo2023, sec3.1_p3).

The rarity problem is further compounded by the nature of the data itself: "the rarity of actual collision events in the historical dataset created a severe class imbalance problem, making it difficult to train supervised learning models that could accurately distinguish between safe and unsafe encounters" (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p1).

## Training Challenges

The scarcity of high-risk events directly impacts model learning capacity. In experimental simulations with small training sets (test size of 0.95), training sets contained merely 523.0 events with only 10.8 high-risk cases (uriot2022, sec6.2_p9). With such "insufficient data to learn from, the models quickly overfit and failed to learn generalizable rules," resulting in a mean 12.61% performance gain on training data but a 7.73% mean loss on test data relative to baseline (uriot2022, sec6.2_p9).

Recognizing this challenge, 65% of competition participants attempted to explicitly address class imbalance through approaches such as "artificially balancing the classes, assigning importance weighing to samples" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3).

## Validation and Generalization Challenges

The rarity of collision events severely complicates validation set construction. Half of competition participants attempted to build validation sets with similar properties and risk distribution as the test set but failed, with "most surveyed teams lamented a poor correlation between training and test set performances" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3).

The validation problem is exacerbated by the non-random sampling strategy employed. The training and test sets were "not randomly sampled from the dataset," with "events corresponding to useful operational scenarios" appearing in the test set (uriot2022, sec4.2_p2). This design choice, while operationally motivated, further complicated the validation challenge.

When test sets were small (test size of 0.05), they contained approximately 523.0 events with only 10.8 high-risk cases, making the test set "no longer representative" (uriot2022, sec6.2_p9). Performance evaluation became highly variable depending on "the 'predictability' of events that ended up on the test set," yielding a mean gain of only 0.04% with a standard deviation of 9.83% (uriot2022, sec6.2_p9).

## Ground Truth Data Limitations

The fundamental challenge of limited verified collision data is acknowledged: "While comprehensive collision datasets remain limited, the theoretical assessment of close conjunction events characterized by non-zero miss distances provides a viable foundation for evaluating the operational validity of AI/ML implementation" (mashiku2025, sec2_p5). This statement suggests that the field must rely on theoretical assessments of near-misses rather than actual collision data for training and validation.

## Interaction with Other Failure Modes

The rarity problem interacts with other characteristics of the data to compound difficulties. The "stochastic and non-linear nature of the conjunction evolution created inconsistent parameter behavior patterns that were difficult for machine learning models to capture reliably," with "sample cases generated from the same baseline often exhibited completely different behavioral patterns, undermining the assumption that historical patterns could reliably predict future conjunction evolution" (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p1).

## Optimal Trade-offs

The experiments revealed that optimal performance required balancing training data quantity with test set representativeness, with "the optimal trade-off lay in a test size of 0.2, where a 6.45% gain in the training set performance over the LRP baseline translated into a 1.12% gain in the test set" (uriot2022, sec6.2_p9).

chunks.authors: Francisco Caldas, Claudia Soares
chunks.text: Since the late 1950s, when the first artificial satellite was launched, the number of Resident Space Objects has steadily increased. It is estimated that around one million objects larger than one cm are currently orbiting the Earth, with only thirty thousand larger than ten cm being tracked. To avert a chain reaction of collisions, known as Kessler Syndrome, it is essential to accurately track and predict debris and satellites' orbits. Current approximate physics-based methods have errors in the order of kilometers for seven-day predictions, which is insufficient when considering space debris, typically with less than one meter. This failure is usually due to uncertainty around the state of the space object at the beginning of the trajectory, forecasting errors in environmental conditions such as atmospheric drag, and unknown characteristics such as the mass or geometry of the space object. Operators can enhance Orbit Prediction accuracy by deriving unmeasured objects' characteristics and improving non-conservative forces' effects by leveraging data-driven techniques, such as Machine Learning. In this survey, we provide an overview of the work in applying Machine Learning for Orbit Determination, Orbit Prediction, and atmospheric density modeling.

chunks.authors: Francisco Caldas, Claudia Soares
chunks.text: Orbit Prediction (OP): Orbit Prediction is the process of predicting the future position and associated uncertainty of any given RSO. Two method families exist for OP: one pursuing analytical solutions [8,9], with the other exploiting numerical approximations [10]. Numerical methods are time-consuming but precise, while analytical methodologies are more straightforward and faster. To be tractable, these algorithms hold simplifying assumptions that hinder accuracy [2]. Each method is limited by OD in that an orbital state with high uncertainty will necessarily evolve to have an inaccurate Orbit Prediction. When used in a Collision Avoidance scheme, this process propagates the state of the RSO until the time of closest approach (TCA) to any actively monitored satellite. The current limitations in Orbit Prediction are the Gaussian assumption – which does not hold against the true distribution [11] – the simplified modeling of perturbation forces, the unknown information regarding RSO characteristics, and the uncertainty over space weather forecast data (see Fig. 1).

chunks.authors: Richard J. Licata, Piyush M. Mehta
chunks.text: In this work, we propose two techniques to develop nonlinear ML regression models to predict thermospheric density while providing robust and reliable uncertainty estimates: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout and direct prediction of the probability distribution, both using the negative logarithm of predictive density (NLPD) loss function. We show the performance capabilities for models trained on both local and global datasets. We show that the NLPD loss provides similar results for both techniques but the direct probability distribution prediction method has a much lower computational cost. For the global model regressed on the Space Environment Technologies High Accuracy Satellite Drag Model (HASDM) density database, we achieve errors of approximately 11% on independent test data with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Using an in-situ CHAllenging Minisatellite Payload (CHAMP) density dataset, models developed using both techniques provide test error on the order of 13%. The CHAMP models—on validation and test data—are within 2% of perfect calibration for the twenty prediction intervals tested. We show that this model can also be used to obtain global density predictions with uncertainties at a given epoch.

Cimmino, Opromolla, and Fasano [11] used MLT to determine the ballistic coefficients of LEO spacecraft based on orbital data. chunks.authors: Francisco Caldas, Claudia Soares
chunks.text: The increasing volume of space objects in Earth's orbit presents a significant challenge for Space Situational Awareness (SSA). chunks.text: Machine learning (ML) has been applied to space weather problems with increasing frequency in recent years, driven by an influx of in-situ measurements and a desire to improve modeling and forecasting capabilities throughout the field. Space weather originates from solar perturbations and is comprised of the resulting complex variations they cause within the numerous systems between the Sun and Earth. These systems are often tightly coupled and not well understood. This creates a need for skillful models with knowledge about the confidence of their predictions. One example of such a dynamical system highly impacted by space weather is the thermosphere, the neutral region of Earth's upper atmosphere. Our inability to forecast it has severe repercussions in the context of satellite drag and computation of probability of collision between two space objects in low Earth orbit (LEO) for decision making in space operations. Even with (assumed) perfect forecast of model drivers, our incomplete knowledge of the system results in often inaccurate thermospheric neutral mass density predictions. Continuing efforts are being made to improve model accuracy, but density models rarely provide estimates of confidence in predictions.

# How Atmospheric Drag Uncertainty Propagates Through ML-Based Orbit Prediction Pipelines

## Sources of Atmospheric Drag Uncertainty

Atmospheric drag uncertainty originates from several compounding factors. Current approximate physics-based methods have errors in the order of kilometers for seven-day predictions, which fail when considering space debris typically less than one meter in size. These failures stem from uncertainty around the initial state of the space object, forecasting errors in environmental conditions such as atmospheric drag, and unknown characteristics such as mass or geometry (survey_ml_orbit2024, sec0_p1).

The thermospheric density models that drive atmospheric drag calculations have inherent limitations. Empirical models that use space weather indexes for forecasting and estimating local density have a one-sigma accuracy of only 10-15%, depending on the model, solar activity, and location (survey_ml_orbit2024, sec5_p7). Furthermore, forecast errors in the driving features compound these problems—for example, a 10% error in Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) light prediction can result in more than 200 km uncertainty for a given satellite after 7 days (survey_ml_orbit2024, sec5_p7).

## Propagation Through ML-Based Pipelines

ML-based orbit prediction attempts to address these uncertainties through several approaches. The orbit prediction process propagates the state of a Resident Space Object (RSO) until the time of closest approach (TCA) to any actively monitored satellite. Current limitations include the Gaussian assumption (which does not hold against the true distribution), simplified modeling of perturbation forces, unknown information regarding RSO characteristics, and uncertainty over space weather forecast data (survey_ml_orbit2024, sec1_p3).

Traditional orbital prediction methods based on physical models are inaccurate with divergent errors due to challenges in modeling the atmosphere and acquiring physical information of specific spacecraft. Orbit decay predictions also depend on space environment information, which is hard to accurately predict (he2024, sec1_p4).

ML techniques have been proposed to mitigate these issues. One approach uses machine learning to determine ballistic coefficients of LEO spacecraft based on orbital data, which can minimize prediction errors stemming from uncertainties in drag coefficients and area-to-mass ratios (he2024, sec1_p4). Another method employed proximal policy optimization (PPO2) to adjust atmosphere model parameters, resulting in a maximum absolute space position error of 8133.329 m on the CSS in 3 days compared to standard orbital data (he2024, sec1_p4).

Recent work has demonstrated that ML models can achieve approximately 11% errors on independent test data with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates for global models, and approximately 13% test error for local in-situ density datasets (licata2022, sec0_p2). Advanced ML techniques using Monte Carlo dropout and direct prediction of probability distributions with the negative logarithm of predictive density (NLPD) loss function have been developed to provide robust and reliable uncertainty estimates (licata2022, sec0_p2).

## Downstream Effects on Collision Probability Estimates

The evidence provided does not directly detail how atmospheric drag uncertainty quantitatively affects collision probability calculations in ML-based systems. However, the NASA handbook addresses this issue for traditional methods: atmospheric density forecast error has been studied by comparing predicted densities (using predicted space weather indices) to actual densities and producing polynomial fits of the relative density error as a function of satellite perigee height and space weather indices. These fits produce a variance term that can be added to the ballistic coefficient variance in the covariance (nasa_ca_handbook2023, sec16.7.1_p3).

The inability to forecast thermospheric density has severe repercussions in the context of satellite drag and computation of probability of collision between two space objects in low Earth orbit (LEO) for decision making in space operations. Even with perfect forecast of model drivers, incomplete knowledge of the system results in often inaccurate thermospheric neutral mass density predictions (licata2022, sec0_p1).

## Information Gaps

The provided evidence does not contain specific quantitative analyses of:
1. How uncertainty estimates from ML-based atmospheric density models propagate through the full orbit prediction pipeline to collision probability calculations
2. Comparative studies showing collision probability accuracy differences between traditional and ML-based approaches
3. Specific methodologies for incorporating ML-based uncertainty estimates into conjunction assessment workflows
4. Statistical validation of collision probability estimates when using ML-predicted atmospheric densities versus traditional models

Additional sources needed would include studies on conjunction assessment with ML-based orbit predictions, specific collision probability calculation methodologies incorporating ML uncertainty quantification, and operational validation studies comparing collision warning accuracy between different approaches.

---

# ML Architectures Applied to CDM Time-Series Prediction and Their Failure Modes

## Architectures Applied

Several ML architectures have been tested for CDM (Conjunction Data Message) time-series prediction:

### 1. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs)
BNNs have been tested for their suitability in space domain awareness (SDA) tasks, particularly for managing uncertainty and predicting the future (rand_ai_ssa2024, sec5_p1). Specifically, Bayesian recurrent neural networks have been developed to predict the contents of future CDMs in conjunction events, conditioned on all CDMs received up to that point, with associated uncertainty estimates (acciarini2021, sec0_p3).

### 2. LSTM Networks
Manhattan LSTMs showed good performance during the Collision Avoidance Challenge (CAC) (catulo2023, sec1_p6). LSTM models were designed specifically for time-series prediction using multiple CDM time-series datasets (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 3. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs)
ANNs have been used to approximate prediction errors based on learning variables, where the model generates ML-predicted errors that ideally should equal true prediction errors (peng2018, sec2.3_p4).

### 4. Gradient Boosting Trees
Gradient boosting trees (specifically LightGBM) demonstrated good performance during the CAC (catulo2023, sec1_p6). LightGBM was used with numerical features from CDMs, with the algorithm addressing missing values through its own internal mechanisms (uriot2022, sec6.1_p1).

### 5. Shallow Binary Classification Networks
Shallow neural networks showed marginal improvements in risk classification when incorporating multiple information parameters beyond just collision probability (Pc) (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 6. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs)
HMMs were used with only the risk parameter considered from CDMs arranged in descending order regarding time to predicted TCA (catulo2023, sec3.3_p3).

## Failure Modes and Performance Issues

### 1. Poor Generalization
Deep Neural Networks, particularly LSTM models designed for time-series prediction, "suffered from insufficient 'ground truth data' for training and poor generalization to diverse conjunction scenarios" (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 2. Marginal Improvement Over Baselines
The competition revealed that "the naive/baseline approach (using the risk contained in the last CDM received until the cut-off time as the risk prediction) is a strong predictor for this problem, with only 12 teams out of 97 managing to beat the benchmark solution" (catulo2023, sec1_p6). Shallow binary classification networks showed "extremely marginal" improvement compared to using normal Pc thresholds, "raising questions about the practical value of the additional computational complexity" (mashiku2025, sec5.1_p2).

### 3. Under-utilization of Temporal Information
A critical failure mode was the tendency to ignore temporal information: "65% of the teams framed the learning problem as a static one, summarizing the information contained in the time series as an aggregation of attributes (e.g., using summary statistics, or simply the latest available CDM)" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p4). This may have been "a direct consequence of the great predictive strength of a naive forecast for this dataset" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p4).

### 4. Residual Prediction Errors
For ANN models, while the goal was for ML-predicted errors to equal true prediction errors (making residual error zero), "in practice, the statistical properties of e_res(tj; ti) will be analyzed to evaluate the performance of the trained ANN model," suggesting that residual errors persist (peng2018, sec2.3_p4).

## Missing Information

The evidence provided does not include:
- Quantitative comparison metrics between different architectures
- Specific failure rates or error distributions for each approach
- Detailed analysis of why LSTMs fail to generalize despite being theoretically appropriate for time-series data
- Information about overfitting vs. underfitting tendencies across architectures
- Computational cost comparisons that might explain the preference for simpler models

Sources comparing transformer-based architectures or more recent deep learning approaches would be helpful for a more complete picture.

Generation of Orbital Decay Training Set

chunks.authors: Richard J. Licata, Piyush M. Mehta
chunks.text: Even with these improvements, density models have high errors, and we generally use them without any knowledge of their confidence given the conditions. Until recently, no thermospheric density models—whether physics-based or empirical—provided estimates of uncertainty. Bruinsma et al. developed an uncertainty-based version of DTM2020 using polynomials to describe the 1 − sigma uncertainties as a function of the inputs. Licata et al. used MC dropout to obtain uncertainty estimates for a global density modeling application with good calibration, providing baseline performance. In this work, we leverage machine learning (ML) to generate predictive density models for the thermosphere that also provide robust and reliable uncertainty estimates. This is done for both a global and local datasets using two methods: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout and a direct prediction of the probability distribution (referred to primarily as direct probability).

chunks.authors: Richard J. Licata, Piyush M. Mehta
chunks.text: In this work, we leverage the NLPD loss function to develop thermospheric density models using (1) MC dropout and (2) direct probability prediction. These two uncertainty techniques were used to create both a model based in the PCA coefficients of the SET HASDM density database and a model based in localized accelerometer-derived density estimates from CHAMP. Using two toy problems, we showed that the NLPD loss function can be used to create a ML model with calibrated uncertainty estimates relative to uncertainty in the model, uncertainty in the data, or both. For the HASDM database, the MC dropout and direct probability distribution prediction models had similar metrics in terms of error and calibration. Furthermore, the calibration curves for the PCA coefficients were nearly identical. By looking at the density calibration of both HASDM models, we found that they were well-calibrated at mid-altitudes, and there was more lateral variability in the calibration of the MC dropout model.

chunks.authors: Richard J. Licata, Piyush M. Mehta
chunks.text: In this work, we propose two techniques to develop nonlinear ML regression models to predict thermospheric density while providing robust and reliable uncertainty estimates: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout and direct prediction of the probability distribution, both using the negative logarithm of predictive density (NLPD) loss function. # Catastrophic Forgetting in Orbit Decay Prediction

## The Problem

Catastrophic forgetting presents a significant challenge for machine learning techniques in orbit decay prediction. According to He et al., "The dynamic factors influencing the decay, such as the space environment and spacecraft physical parameters, pose a challenge of catastrophic forgetting for conventional MLT" (he2024, sec1_p6). This limitation affects the generalization capabilities of current model-agnostic machine learning techniques (he2024, sec1_p6).

The study explains that catastrophic forgetting blocks "generalization performance of machine learning techniques (MLTs)" in precise orbit decay prediction (PODP), resulting in "limited improvement on PODP" (he2024, sec0_p1). This is particularly problematic because orbit decay is influenced by varying dynamic factors including space environment conditions and spacecraft physical parameters.

## He 2024's Solution: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)

To address catastrophic forgetting, He et al. (2024) propose the Expandable Orbit Decay Propagator (EODP), which incorporates Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) theory. The paper states that "EODP employs a deep NN (DNN) as the fundamental learner to comprehend the decaying rule and incorporates the theory of EWC" (he2024, sec1_p7).

EWC is described as a regularization-based approach that "combines historical and recent training data to update the NN parameters by applying a penalty function" (he2024, sec1_p6). The authors note that "EWC is particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data" (he2024, sec1_p6), making it appropriate for orbit decay prediction applications where historical orbital data is available.

## Alternative Approaches Considered

He et al. also discuss other strategies that have been explored for enhancing neural network generalization performance, including:

- **Optimization-based methods** like meta-learning, which aims to achieve "learning to learn" and has been used in spacecraft terminal autonomous navigation and control (he2024, sec1_p6)
- **Replay-based techniques** such as experience replay, which creates a memory buffer to retain samples from previous tasks and has been explored in spacecraft collision avoidance (he2024, sec1_p6)

However, the authors chose EWC for their EODP approach, noting that "Meta-learning methods excel in few-shot learning, and experience replay efficiently constructs and utilizes memory buffers with a limited sample size. EWC is particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data" (he2024, sec1_p6).

## Results

The EODP method "achieves at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP)" (he2024, sec0_p1) and "greatly improves prediction accuracy and generalization performance" compared to previous methods (he2024, sec1_p7).

---

# Class Imbalance as a Barrier to ML for Collision Avoidance

## Evidence of Class Imbalance as a Fundamental Barrier

The evidence strongly supports that class imbalance is recognized as a fundamental challenge in applying ML to spacecraft collision avoidance:

**Recognition of the Problem:**
Class imbalance is explicitly identified as a shortcoming of discriminative binary-classification approaches to spacecraft collision avoidance (acciarini2021, sec3.1_p1). The dataset used in the ESA Spacecraft Collision Avoidance Challenge is described as "highly unbalanced" with training and test sets not randomly sampled (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3). More specifically, the dataset contains "only a very small percentage of the events having a final risk higher than −6" (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1), making it "extremely imbalanced" (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1).

**Impact on ML Approaches:**
The class imbalance challenge is characterized as "unavoidable" and derived from "the unavoidable unbalanced nature of the dataset" (uriot2022, sec7_p1). This imbalance was significant enough that "the use of automated, off-the-shelf ML pipelines were limited" (uriot2022, sec7_p1), indicating it posed a substantial barrier to straightforward ML application.

**Performance Implications:**
Most survey respondents "lamented a poor correlation between training and test set performances" when attempting to build validation sets with similar risk distributions to the test set (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3), suggesting the imbalance complicated model development and evaluation.

## Proposed Solutions

**Direct Class Imbalance Mitigation:**
A majority (65%) of competition participants reported explicitly attempting to address class imbalance through approaches such as "artificially balancing the classes" or "assigning importance weighing to samples" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3).

**Data Filtering Strategy:**
One specific solution involved leveraging naive forecast predictions to filter the dataset. When naive forecast predicted a final risk value of −30, 99.34% of predictions were correct without misclassification of high-risk events (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1). By assuming these −30 predictions were trustworthy and removing them from training data, "a significant amount of low-risk conjunctions are removed, which can help deal with the data imbalance problem" while also reducing computational requirements (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1).

**Alternative Problem Formulation:**
Rather than using discriminative binary-classification, researchers focused attention on "generative modeling of the problem" to describe "the temporal evolution of a sequence of CDMs given all previously observed CDMs" (acciarini2021, sec3.1_p1). This reformulation was motivated partly by the class imbalance issue inherent to binary classification approaches.

**Validation Set Construction:**
Half of participants attempted to "build a validation set with similar properties and risk distribution as the test set" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3), though this approach reportedly failed due to poor correlation between training and test performance.

## Limitations in Evidence

While the evidence clearly establishes class imbalance as a recognized barrier and documents several attempted solutions, it does not provide:
- Quantitative comparisons of solution effectiveness
- Detailed descriptions of the artificial balancing or importance weighting methods used
- Success rates or performance improvements from the proposed solutions
- Whether any solution was deemed sufficient for operational use

The evidence suggests that despite these solutions, the fundamental challenge remains unresolved for operational deployment, as "AI/ML approaches investigated to date have not yet demonstrated sufficient reliability for operational collision avoidance decision making" (mashiku2025, sec6_p1).

The effectiveness of the traditional orbital prediction method for PODP is limited by inaccurate estimation of the spacecraft's physical parameters and space environments. Generalization performance of machine learning techniques (MLTs) is blocked by the universal challenge known as catastrophic forgetting, resulting in limited improvement on PODP. In this study, a method of expandable orbit decay propagator (EODP) for spacecraft PODP in VLEO, based on model-agnostic MLTs, is proposed. The plasticity of the proposed model is discussed, which originates from the uncertainty of neural network (NN) parameters. The proposed method overcomes the negative effects of uncertain physical parameters and complex space environments. The model achieves at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP) and presents a novel approach for the future implementation of machine learning–based methods in the field of orbit prediction.

The EWC combines historical and recent training data to update the NN parameters by applying a penalty function, commonly used to process large datasets by decomposing them into several subsets in the field of earth observation [28]. Meta-learning methods excel in few-shot learning, and experience replay efficiently constructs and utilizes memory buffers with a limited sample size. # How Catastrophic Forgetting Affects ML Models for Orbit Decay Prediction

## The Problem of Catastrophic Forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting is identified as a "universal challenge" that blocks the generalization performance of machine learning techniques (MLTs) in orbit decay prediction, resulting in limited improvement on precise orbit decay prediction (PODP) (he2024, sec0_p1). More specifically, the dynamic factors influencing orbit decay—such as the space environment and spacecraft physical parameters—pose a challenge of catastrophic forgetting for conventional MLT (he2024, sec1_p6). This means that as ML models encounter new orbital conditions or spacecraft configurations, they tend to forget previously learned patterns, limiting their ability to generalize across different scenarios.

Due to this phenomenon, current model-agnostic MLTs face limitations in terms of their generalization capabilities (he2024, sec1_p6). This is particularly problematic for orbit decay prediction because spacecraft operate in diverse and changing conditions that require models to maintain knowledge across multiple tasks or scenarios.

## He 2024's Solution: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)

To address catastrophic forgetting, He et al. (2024) propose the Expandable Orbit Decay Propagator (EODP), which employs a deep neural network (DNN) as the fundamental learner and incorporates the theory of Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) (he2024, sec1_p7).

EWC is described as a regularization-based approach that combines historical and recent training data to update the neural network parameters by applying a penalty function (he2024, sec1_p6). The authors note that EWC is particularly suited for regression problems with abundant training data (he2024, sec1_p6), which aligns well with the orbit prediction domain where large amounts of orbital data are available.

The proposed EODP method is stated to overcome the negative effects of uncertain physical parameters and complex space environments, achieving at least a 70% improvement in accuracy compared to the high-precision orbital propagator (HPOP) (he2024, sec0_p1). Compared to previous methods, EODP greatly improves both prediction accuracy and generalization performance (he2024, sec1_p7).

## Context: Alternative Approaches

While He et al. focus on EWC, the evidence indicates that other strategies have been explored to enhance the generalization performance of neural networks, including optimization-based methods (like meta-learning) and replay-based techniques (such as experience replay) (he2024, sec1_p6). However, the choice of EWC appears driven by its suitability for regression problems with abundant training data, distinguishing it from meta-learning (which excels in few-shot learning) and experience replay (which efficiently utilizes limited sample sizes) (he2024, sec1_p6).

# REFERENCES

# Operational Challenges for ML Integration in Conjunction Assessment

NASA and its partners have identified several significant operational challenges for integrating machine learning into conjunction assessment workflows:

## Data and Reliability Challenges

The investigation revealed **fundamental limitations due to stochasticity of the data, the complex and stochastic nature of orbital mechanics, and the difficulty in achieving the high reliability and explainability standards required for high-value, high-risk space operations decision-making** (mashiku2025, sec5_p1). The research concluded that **significant advances in data collection, model interpretability, and validation methodologies would be required before machine learning techniques could be considered viable for operational conjunction assessment applications** (mashiku2025, sec5.3_p3).

A critical data challenge is the **limited availability of verified ground truth data, as comprehensive collision datasets remain limited**, though theoretical assessment of close conjunction events with non-zero miss distances can provide a foundation for evaluating ML operational validity (mashiku2025, sec2_p5).

## Explainability Requirements

The **"explainability" paradox inherent in many machine learning approaches posed significant concerns for operational implementation, as conjunction assessment decisions require clear justification and understanding of the underlying reasons and factors for each outcome** (mashiku2025, sec5_p1). This need for explainability is emphasized as a requirement for **facilitating operator-machine teaming and operator trust** (rand_ai_ssa2024, sec0_p3).

## Validation and Performance Requirements

Machine learning approaches **showed theoretical promise for enhancing conjunction assessment capabilities**, but **significant additional work would be needed to overcome stochastic data limitations, improve model interpretability, and demonstrate reliable performance via validation across the full spectrum of operational conjunction scenarios before these methods could be considered for operational deployment** (mashiku2025, sec5_p1).

## Operational Scope Limitations

Current assessment indicates that **fully automated AI/ML decision systems are not currently viable for operational risk assessment** (mashiku2025, sec6_p3). The research suggests that ML may be better suited for **identifying which conjunction events deserve analyst attention, rather than performing risk assessments and conclusive early decision-support for mitigative maneuver decisions** (mashiku2025, sec6_p3).

## Workload and Scaling Pressures

The operational context includes significant workload pressures. **Conjunction assessment workload is a function of: the total number of CDMs received, the number of events with risk levels requiring enhanced monitoring, and the number requiring mitigation planning and potential execution** (nasa_ca_handbook2023, sec9_p1). As **large constellations continue to launch, the need for more sophisticated automation becomes increasingly urgent, but such automation must maintain the high reliability standards required for space operations** (mashiku2025, sec6_p3).

## Data Integration Complexity

Additional operational difficulties arise from **receiving higher-level products from commercial vendors, such as vectors or even conjunction assessment outputs like CDMs, which introduces multiple solutions into the enterprise and creates significant operational difficulties in trying to adjudicate among them** (nasa_ca_handbook2023, sec14.1_p2).

## Future Path Forward

The research suggests that **hybrid approaches combining traditional physics-based methods with targeted machine learning components may offer incremental improvements** (mashiku2025, sec6_p3), and **by carefully constraining the problem domain and setting realistic expectations, future AI/ML approaches may yet find valuable niches within the broader conjunction assessment workflow, even if they cannot yet replace traditional physics-based methods entirely** (mashiku2025, sec6_p4).

# Class Imbalance as a Barrier to ML for Collision Avoidance

## Evidence of Class Imbalance as a Fundamental Barrier

The evidence consistently identifies class imbalance as a significant challenge in applying ML to spacecraft collision avoidance:

**Recognition as a Core Problem**: The dataset for collision avoidance is described as "highly unbalanced" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3), and this imbalance is characterized as "unavoidable" in nature (uriot2022, sec7_p1). The discriminative binary-classification formulation of the problem (high- vs low-risk events) has been specifically criticized for "training data class imbalance" among other shortcomings (acciarini2021, sec3.1_p1).

**Severity of Imbalance**: The dataset is described as "extremely imbalanced with only a very small percentage of the events having a final risk higher than −6" (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1). This extreme imbalance appears to be inherent to the operational reality of collision avoidance, where truly high-risk events are rare.

**Impact on Model Performance**: The competition results revealed that "the training and test sets not randomly sampled from the dataset" contributed to difficulties, with "most surveyed teams lamented a poor correlation between training and test set performances" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3). This suggests that the imbalanced nature of the data creates challenges in building generalizable models.

**Operational Reliability Concerns**: The imbalance problem contributes to broader reliability concerns, with one source noting that "AI/ML approaches investigated to date have not yet demonstrated sufficient reliability for operational collision avoidance decision making" (mashiku2025, sec6_p1).

## Proposed Solutions

Several approaches have been proposed or implemented to address class imbalance:

**1. Explicit Balancing Techniques**: A majority (65%) of competition participants "explicitly attempted to address class imbalance (e.g., by artificially balancing the classes, assigning importance weighing to samples)" (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3).

**2. Generative Modeling Approach**: Rather than using discriminative classification, researchers have focused "attention on the generative modeling of the problem" to "describe the temporal evolution of a sequence of CDMs given all previously observed CDMs" (acciarini2021, sec3.1_p1). This approach aims to sidestep some issues inherent in binary classification with imbalanced data.

**3. Selective Training Strategy**: One documented solution involves filtering out the most obvious low-risk cases. Specifically, when the naive forecast predicts a final risk of −30, "99.34% of the predictions are correct without any misclassification of high-risk events," leading researchers to exclude these events from training and "directly predicted with a final risk of −30" during testing (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1). This approach "help[s] deal with the data imbalance problem" while reducing computational requirements (catulo2023, sec3.3_p1).

**4. Validation Set Construction**: Half of competition participants "reported attempting to build a validation set with similar properties and risk distribution as the test set," though this approach largely failed (uriot2022, sec5.1_p3).

**5. Alternative Prediction Targets**: Some researchers have explored "predict[ing] the final chaser position uncertainties for each event and used those predictions to compute the risk" rather than directly predicting risk (catulo2023, sec1_p7).

## Limitations in Evidence

The evidence does not provide:
- Quantitative comparisons of the effectiveness of different balancing approaches
- Detailed analysis of why validation set construction attempts failed
- Specific technical details on artificial balancing or importance weighting methods used
- Long-term operational results demonstrating whether any solution has achieved production-level reliability
